subtopic_detail: Arranging trauma focused therapy for a patient with limited English after a partial response to medication
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 35-year-old woman who arrived in Australia four years ago as a refugee and was granted a permanent visa eighteen months ago. Speaking through a professional interpreter, she describes nightmares almost every night, sudden intrusive images of events in a detention setting, and avoiding the supermarket because the lighting brings the images back.

She lives in stable public housing with her adult daughter, uses no alcohol or other substances, and has no current thoughts of self harm. She is not in contact with anyone who threatens her and has no outstanding legal or immigration matters.

She has taken sertraline 100 mg daily for eight months with good adherence, and reports her sleep has improved a little and the daytime irritability has settled, but the nightmares and intrusive images are unchanged. Her conversational English is limited to short exchanges and she asks her daughter to translate when she attends her general practitioner.

data_table.Mental state: Nightmares, intrusive imagery, avoidance of supermarket lighting, hyperarousal partially improved; no suicidal ideation
data_table.Current treatment: Sertraline 100 mg orally daily for eight months with good adherence and partial response
data_table.Psychosocial: Stable public housing, permanent visa granted, no ongoing threat, no legal or immigration matters outstanding
data_table.Substance use: No alcohol or other substance use
data_table.Language: Limited conversational English; attends with her adult daughter translating at the general practice

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her treatment?

options.text: Increase the sertraline to 200 mg daily and review her again in eight weeks
options.rationale: Dose escalation is reasonable when psychological therapy is unavailable or declined, and medication is a second-line option in post-traumatic stress disorder rather than the treatment with the best effect size. Escalating without offering the more effective intervention accepts a partial response unnecessarily. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for trauma focused psychological therapy with her daughter interpreting
options.rationale: Using a family member as interpreter is not acceptable practice in any clinical setting and is particularly damaging in trauma work, where the patient will censor disclosure to protect the relative and the relative may be re-traumatised or may filter the content. Professional interpreters are engaged even when the family offers to help. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Add low dose quetiapine at night for the nightmares and review in eight weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotic augmentation has limited evidence in post-traumatic stress disorder and carries metabolic and sedative burden, so it sits well down the list of options. Prazosin has better evidence specifically for nightmares if a pharmacological adjunct is needed after trauma focused therapy has been offered. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for generic supportive counselling delivered in English at the practice
options.rationale: Non-directive supportive counselling performs no better than waiting list in post-traumatic stress disorder and is specifically not recommended as a substitute for trauma focused therapy. Delivering it in a language she cannot follow compounds the problem. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for trauma focused psychological therapy with a professional interpreter
options.rationale: Trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing are the first-line treatments with the largest effect sizes, and she has the stability in housing, immigration status and substance use that makes trauma processing appropriate now. A professional interpreter, ideally the same one across sessions and briefed about the content, is essential so that she can disclose freely and the therapy retains its fidelity. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Australian guidelines place trauma focused psychological therapies, principally trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing, ahead of pharmacotherapy for post-traumatic stress disorder on the strength of their effect sizes. Medication is offered when psychological therapy is unavailable, declined or insufficient, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are the usual first choice. Trauma processing requires a baseline of safety and stability, meaning the person is not living under continuing threat, has somewhere to live, and is not in uncontrolled substance withdrawal; where those conditions are absent, practical and stabilisation work comes first. For people from refugee backgrounds the assessment must also consider the effects of the settlement process itself, including visa insecurity, family separation and the loss of occupational identity, all of which can maintain symptoms independently of the original trauma. Engaging a professional interpreter, rather than a family member, is a requirement of safe and effective care and is arranged as a matter of course rather than on request.
key_points: Trauma focused psychological therapy is first line and outperforms medication
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are second line; supportive counselling is not recommended
Trauma processing requires baseline safety and stability in housing, threat and substance use
Never use a family member as interpreter, particularly in trauma work
Settlement stressors such as visa insecurity and family separation maintain symptoms independently
explanation.pearls: Prazosin, titrated from 1 mg at night, has the best evidence of any drug specifically for trauma related nightmares, and the dose-limiting problem is first dose postural hypotension rather than any central effect.

sources.label: Foundation House: Working with interpreters in mental health

subtopic_detail: Acute toxicity from an unregulated smoking product with a negative routine urine drug immunoassay
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar receiving a 22-year-old man brought in by ambulance from a share house. His flatmate says he smoked 'a herbal blend he bought off a website' about ninety minutes ago and then became terrified, shouting that the walls were closing in.

En route he vomited repeatedly and had a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting about forty seconds that terminated without treatment. He is now agitated, pacing and pulling at the monitoring leads, and will not sit for examination.

His pupils are 6 mm and reactive, he is diaphoretic and his skin is flushed. A urine drug immunoassay is negative for amphetamines, delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, cocaine metabolites, opioids and benzodiazepines. Point of care glucose is 6.1 mmol/L and the electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with a corrected QT interval of 430 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 146/min, blood pressure 168/96 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 38.4°C
data_table.Examination: Agitated and pacing, pupils 6 mm and reactive, diaphoretic, flushed skin
data_table.Investigations: Urine immunoassay negative for amphetamines, delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, cocaine metabolites, opioids and benzodiazepines; glucose 6.1 mmol/L
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus tachycardia, corrected QT interval 430 ms
data_table.Event: One generalised tonic-clonic seizure of about 40 seconds, self-terminating, 90 minutes after smoking an online herbal product

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intramuscular haloperidol 10 mg and repeat the dose after thirty minutes
options.rationale: Butyrophenones lower the seizure threshold, impair thermoregulation and prolong the corrected QT interval, all of which are active hazards in a patient who has already seized and is hyperthermic. Antipsychotics are second line in stimulant-type toxicity and only after adequate benzodiazepine loading. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give intravenous naloxone 400 micrograms and repeat the dose after two minutes
options.rationale: Opioid toxicity presents with pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression and reduced conscious state, which is the opposite of this hyperadrenergic picture with 6 mm pupils and tachypnoea. Naloxone would achieve nothing and would precipitate withdrawal if opioids were also on board. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give oral activated charcoal 50 g and observe him in the short stay unit
options.rationale: Charcoal has no role after an inhaled exposure, since the drug has bypassed the gut entirely, and administering it to an agitated patient risks aspiration. Decontamination is relevant to recent large oral ingestions with a protected airway. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Titrate intravenous diazepam to sedation with supportive cooling measures
options.rationale: Synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonists are full agonists at the cannabinoid receptor, far more potent than delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, and are not detected by the routine immunoassay, which is why a negative screen in a classic presentation does not exclude them. Treatment is supportive with titrated benzodiazepine sedation, which simultaneously controls agitation, raises the seizure threshold, reduces the adrenergic drive and lowers heat generation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg and repeat the dose after thirty minutes
options.rationale: Olanzapine is a reasonable adjunct once benzodiazepines have been loaded and agitation persists, and it is not the first agent when seizures and hyperthermia are present. Its anticholinergic burden also impairs sweating in a patient who is already at 38.4 degrees. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonists are sprayed onto plant material and sold as herbal smoking blends, and their toxicity differs sharply from that of cannabis because they are full rather than partial agonists at the cannabinoid receptor and carry no cannabidiol to moderate the effect. The clinical picture includes severe agitation, psychosis, vomiting, seizures, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, and occasionally acute kidney injury or myocardial ischaemia, which are essentially unseen with cannabis itself. Routine urine immunoassays target delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol metabolites and do not cross-react with these compounds, so a negative cannabis screen is expected and must not be used to exclude the exposure. The chemical structures are altered continually to stay ahead of scheduling, which means potency and effect vary unpredictably between batches sold under the same brand name. Management is supportive, centred on titrated benzodiazepine sedation, active cooling, fluids, and monitoring for rhabdomyolysis and renal impairment.
key_points: Synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonists are full agonists and far more potent than cannabis
Routine urine immunoassay does not detect them, so a negative screen is uninformative
Seizures, hyperthermia and severe agitation distinguish them from cannabis intoxication
Titrated benzodiazepine sedation is the first-line treatment, not an antipsychotic
Monitor for rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury after significant agitation or hyperthermia
explanation.pearls: Check a creatine kinase and renal function in anyone sedated after synthetic cannabinoid toxicity: acute kidney injury has been reported in clusters with these products even without prolonged struggling or marked hyperthermia.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Synthetic cannabinoid toxicity

subtopic_detail: New onset shoplifting in middle age with preserved memory and a near normal cognitive screen
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 58-year-old accountant referred by the court liaison service after a third shoplifting charge in six months. Each time he walked out of a supermarket with items he could easily afford and did not need, and each time he seemed puzzled rather than concerned when stopped.

His wife, seen separately, says that over about two years he has become 'a different person'. He tells strangers their clothes are unflattering, stood too close to a neighbour's teenage daughter at a barbecue, and laughed when their dog died. He has started eating four or five sweet pastries a day and has gained 11 kg. He no longer initiates conversation at home and watches the same programme repeatedly.

He denies low mood, sleeps well and has a normal appetite pattern apart from the sweet food. He scores 26 out of 30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, losing points only on verbal fluency and abstraction, and recalls all five delayed words without cueing. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain, arranged by the general practitioner, is reported as bilateral frontal and anterior temporal atrophy.

data_table.Behavioural change: Disinhibited remarks, loss of social awareness, absent empathy, compulsive repetitive viewing, apathy with loss of conversational initiation
data_table.Dietary change: Four to five sweet pastries daily with 11 kg weight gain
data_table.Mood and sleep: No low mood reported, sleep pattern unchanged, no anhedonia described
data_table.Cognition: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 26 out of 30, points lost on verbal fluency and abstraction only; five of five delayed words recalled without cueing
data_table.Imaging: Magnetic resonance imaging reports bilateral frontal and anterior temporal atrophy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a specialist cognitive and neurology service for further assessment
options.rationale: Progressive disinhibition, loss of empathy, apathy, compulsive repetitive behaviour and hyperorality with carbohydrate craving are the core diagnostic features of behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia, and the imaging corroborates them. Memory is characteristically preserved early, so a near normal cognitive screen argues for the diagnosis rather than against it, and specialist assessment is needed for neuropsychology, genetic counselling and medicolegal input into the charges. (Source: Dementia Australia: Frontotemporal dementia)

options.text: Diagnose kleptomania and refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for impulses
options.rationale: Kleptomania requires rising tension before the theft and relief or gratification afterwards, with the person recognising the act as wrong, and it typically begins in adolescence or early adulthood. He shows puzzlement rather than tension or remorse, and the onset in middle age alongside other behavioural change points to an acquired cause. (Source: Dementia Australia: Frontotemporal dementia)

options.text: Start naltrexone for the impulsive behaviour and review him in eight weeks
options.rationale: Opioid antagonists are used for impulse control disorders such as gambling and are not a treatment for behaviour arising from frontal degeneration. Treating the symptom pharmacologically without establishing the cause would also leave the driving, financial and medicolegal consequences unaddressed. (Source: Dementia Australia: Frontotemporal dementia)

options.text: Start an antidepressant for a depressive episode and review him in eight weeks
options.rationale: Apathy in frontotemporal dementia is frequently misread as depression, and this is the commonest initial misdiagnosis, but he reports no low mood, no sleep disturbance and no anhedonia, and apathy without subjective sadness is the distinguishing pattern. Serotonergic agents can help the compulsive and disinhibited behaviours later but do not substitute for making the diagnosis. (Source: Dementia Australia: Frontotemporal dementia)

options.text: Refer to forensic psychiatry for an assessment of feigned cognitive symptoms
options.rationale: Feigning would be a consideration if the presentation had begun after the charges and served an obvious external incentive, whereas his wife dates the change to two years before any legal involvement. Structural imaging showing focal atrophy also provides objective corroboration that exaggeration cannot produce. (Source: Dementia Australia: Frontotemporal dementia)

explanation.summary: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia is the commonest cause of dementia with onset before 60 years and is defined by progressive change in personality and social conduct rather than by amnesia. The diagnostic criteria require three of six features: behavioural disinhibition, apathy or inertia, loss of sympathy or empathy, perseverative or compulsive behaviour, hyperorality or dietary change, and a dysexecutive neuropsychological profile with relative sparing of memory and visuospatial function. That sparing is precisely why bedside screening tools perform poorly, since instruments weighted towards memory and orientation can return a near normal score in a person whose social functioning has collapsed, and the commonest misdiagnoses are depression, bipolar disorder and a primary personality disorder. New onset criminal behaviour in middle age, particularly theft, trespass and sexually inappropriate conduct, is a recognised presentation and carries obvious medicolegal implications for culpability and for driving. Around 40 per cent of cases have a family history and a significant proportion carry mutations in the C9orf72, MAPT or GRN genes, so genetic counselling is part of specialist assessment.
key_points: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia presents with conduct change, not memory loss
Diagnosis needs three of six features including disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy and hyperorality
A near normal Montreal Cognitive Assessment does not exclude it, as memory is spared early
New onset criminal behaviour in middle age is a recognised presentation
A family history is present in around 40 per cent, so genetic counselling forms part of assessment
explanation.pearls: Cholinesterase inhibitors are not indicated in frontotemporal dementia and can worsen disinhibition and agitation, which is the opposite of their effect in Alzheimer disease, so an empirical trial while awaiting the specialist opinion is actively unhelpful.

subtopic_detail: Timeframe for colonoscopy after a positive immunochemical faecal occult blood test in the national program
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 62-year-old man who has brought in a letter reporting a positive result from his National Bowel Cancer Screening Program kit. He completed it three weeks ago and says he 'nearly threw the envelope out because I feel completely fine'.

He has no rectal bleeding, no change in bowel habit and no abdominal pain. His weight has been stable for years. There is no family history of bowel cancer or polyps and he has never had a colonoscopy.

He takes perindopril for hypertension and no antiplatelet or anticoagulant drugs. Examination including abdominal and rectal examination is unremarkable. A full blood count taken last month for another reason showed a haemoglobin of 148 g/L (130-180) with a mean cell volume of 89 fL (80-98).

data_table.Screening result: Positive immunochemical faecal occult blood test through the National Bowel Cancer Screening Program
data_table.Symptoms: No rectal bleeding, no change in bowel habit, no abdominal pain, weight stable
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-180), mean cell volume 89 fL (80-98)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the immunochemical faecal occult blood test in twelve months time
options.rationale: A positive screening test is not repeated to confirm it, because a repeat negative does not exclude the lesion that caused the original bleed and intermittent bleeding from a tumour is the rule rather than the exception. Repeat testing is for people whose kit was inadequate or spoiled. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography colonography within the next thirty days
options.rationale: Computed tomography colonography is the alternative when colonoscopy is incomplete, refused or unsafe, and it cannot take biopsies or remove polyps, so any abnormality still requires colonoscopy afterwards. It is not the first choice in a fit 62-year-old. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines

options.text: Refer for colonoscopy to be performed within thirty days of the result
options.rationale: Around one in 20 people with a positive immunochemical faecal occult blood test has a colorectal cancer and about a third have an advanced adenoma, so colonoscopy is the required follow-up test regardless of whether symptoms are present. Australian guidance is that it should occur within 30 days of the positive result, and outcomes worsen measurably once the interval exceeds about 120 days. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines

options.text: Check a full blood count and iron studies and refer only if he is anaemic
options.rationale: Anaemia is neither sensitive nor specific for colorectal neoplasia, and most screen-detected cancers are found in people with a normal haemoglobin, as his result illustrates. Using a normal blood count to withhold colonoscopy is a recognised route to delayed diagnosis. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines

options.text: Refer for flexible sigmoidoscopy to be performed within thirty days
options.rationale: Sigmoidoscopy examines only to the splenic flexure and would miss the proximal lesions that account for a substantial minority of screen-detected cancers. The whole colon must be visualised after a positive faecal occult blood test. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines

explanation.summary: The National Bowel Cancer Screening Program offers a free immunochemical faecal occult blood test every two years, with eligibility now extending from age 45 to 74 following the lowering of the starting age. The test detects human globin and so does not require dietary restriction, unlike the older guaiac based tests. Participation remains well below target and a substantial number of positive results are never followed up with colonoscopy, which is the single greatest weakness in the program and where general practice makes the most difference. Roughly 5 per cent of positive tests correspond to a cancer and a further third to an advanced adenoma, and the absence of symptoms carries no reassurance because the program exists precisely to find disease before symptoms appear. Colonoscopy is recommended within 30 days, with evidence of worsening stage at diagnosis and survival as the interval lengthens beyond about 120 days.
key_points: A positive immunochemical faecal occult blood test requires colonoscopy, not a repeat test
Target interval is within 30 days, with outcomes worsening beyond about 120 days
About 5 per cent of positive tests correspond to a cancer and a third to an advanced adenoma
Absence of symptoms and a normal haemoglobin do not reduce the need for colonoscopy
The program now covers ages 45 to 74 with two yearly testing
explanation.pearls: The immunochemical test detects human globin and is therefore specific to lower gastrointestinal bleeding, because globin from an upper gastrointestinal source is digested before reaching the colon; this is why it needs no dietary preparation and why a positive result should not be attributed to reflux or peptic ulcer disease.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Colorectal cancer guidelines

subtopic_detail: Choosing a repeat intravenous iron preparation after symptomatic hypophosphataemia from the previous infusion
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a haematology clinic seeing a 44-year-old woman with iron deficiency anaemia from heavy menstrual bleeding. She has a levonorgestrel intrauterine system in place and is awaiting gynaecological review.

Oral ferrous sulfate caused severe nausea and constipation at every dose she tried, including alternate day dosing, and she stopped it after two months. She was given an intravenous infusion of ferric carboxymaltose three months ago.

Two weeks after that infusion she developed profound fatigue, aching in both thighs and pain in her ribs when she coughed, and a serum phosphate taken at the time was 0.42 mmol/L. The symptoms and the phosphate normalised over eight weeks without specific treatment. Her haemoglobin has now fallen again and she needs further parenteral iron.

data_table.Current investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (115-155), mean cell volume 72 fL (80-98), ferritin 8 microgram/L (15-200), transferrin saturation 6 per cent (15-45)
data_table.Previous episode: Serum phosphate 0.42 mmol/L (0.75-1.50) two weeks after ferric carboxymaltose, with fatigue, thigh ache and rib pain; normalised over eight weeks
data_table.Oral iron history: Ferrous sulfate caused severe nausea and constipation including on alternate day dosing; stopped after two months
data_table.Renal and bone profile: Creatinine, corrected calcium and vitamin D within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat ferric carboxymaltose and check the serum phosphate two weeks later
options.rationale: Repeating the same preparation reproduces the mechanism that caused the problem, since ferric carboxymaltose raises intact fibroblast growth factor 23 and drives renal phosphate wasting, and recurrence rates on rechallenge are high. Monitoring the phosphate detects the complication rather than preventing it. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Give ferric derisomaltose instead and check the serum phosphate afterwards
options.rationale: Ferric carboxymaltose is the intravenous iron most strongly associated with fibroblast growth factor 23 mediated hypophosphataemia, and head to head trials show substantially lower rates with ferric derisomaltose, which delivers an equivalent single high dose. Switching preparation addresses the mechanism while still correcting the iron deficit in one visit, with a phosphate check to confirm the change has worked. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Restart oral ferrous sulfate daily and check the haemoglobin in three months
options.rationale: She has already failed oral iron on intolerance grounds including a trial of alternate day dosing, which is the usual strategy for improving tolerance and absorption. Returning to it would leave her anaemic while ongoing menstrual losses continue. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Give oral phosphate supplements and repeat the ferric carboxymaltose today
options.rationale: Oral phosphate does not prevent the renal wasting driven by fibroblast growth factor 23 and can worsen it by further stimulating the hormone. Supplementation is used to treat symptomatic hypophosphataemia once it has occurred, not to enable a rechallenge. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Transfuse two units of red cells and check the serum ferritin afterwards
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise or symptomatic anaemia that cannot wait for iron repletion, and a stable woman with a haemoglobin of 96 g/L does not meet that threshold. It also fails to replenish the iron stores that the marrow needs. (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines)
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines

explanation.summary: Intravenous iron is indicated when oral iron is not tolerated or not absorbed, when losses exceed what oral replacement can match, or when repletion is needed quickly before surgery. Hypophosphataemia is an under-recognised complication that is specific to certain carbohydrate shells, occurring because they increase intact fibroblast growth factor 23, which causes renal phosphate wasting and suppresses calcitriol. It is far more frequent with ferric carboxymaltose than with ferric derisomaltose, iron sucrose or iron polymaltose, and although most cases are asymptomatic and transient, repeated infusions can produce persistent hypophosphataemia with proximal myopathy, bone pain and osteomalacic fractures. Phosphate is checked a fortnight after infusion in anyone receiving repeated doses, in malabsorption, malnutrition or vitamin D deficiency, and in those with existing bone disease. All modern preparations carry a low rate of hypersensitivity and the transient Fishbane reaction of flushing and back or chest tightness, which settles with stopping the infusion and does not by itself contraindicate re-exposure.
key_points: Hypophosphataemia after intravenous iron is mediated by fibroblast growth factor 23
The risk is substantially higher with ferric carboxymaltose than with other preparations
Repeated exposure can cause proximal myopathy, bone pain and osteomalacic fracture
Check phosphate about two weeks after infusion in those needing repeated doses
Switching preparation, rather than supplementing phosphate, is the way to prevent recurrence
explanation.pearls: The Fishbane reaction of facial flushing with chest or back tightness during an iron infusion is not anaphylaxis: there is no urticaria, wheeze or hypotension, and it settles within minutes of pausing the infusion, which can then be restarted at a slower rate.

sources.label: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines
BMJ Best Practice: Iron deficiency anaemia
